title: Python: operations, credentials and readiness
summary: The operations, credentials and readiness code is careful where it matters most. Credentials are sealed with AES-GCM bound to their row identity, the master key is never regenerated, resolved keys refuse serialization, logs redact secrets and keep only exception types, and remote tracing is forced off at every entry point. The worker sends heartbeats on its own connection and drains within a time limit, and the paid trials write each call's worst case to an fsync'd, locked ledger before sending it. The main maintainability cost is rules that exist twice and have already drifted. The trials price calls with their own float parser instead of the catalog's Decimal one, which breaks the DH-06 money rule. The worker's routine-admission gate leaves out the schema check that the API's gate applies. Paid-call settlement is copied five times with different exception scope and state names, and three catalog checks catch different errors. Layering is inverted around operations/: nine modules in application, adapters and api import its logger, application imports the worker, and the worker imports api.main. application/operations.py (501 lines) and route_qualification.py (732 lines) now mix several concerns each. browse_trial.run_trial (192 lines) is never run offline, and the status vocabularies are bare strings held together by six type: ignore comments. Errors are typed and carry no secrets, but four problems remain: the credential store leaks decryption errors to seven callers, boundary logs drop where the error happened, CLI exit codes disagree, and owner bootstrap can't resume after a half-finished run. I read the size leads for provider_settings.py (344 lines) and worker.py (342 lines) and judged both cohesive. Their problems are typing, hidden writes and misplaced wiring, not size.

scores.why: Project ruff and mypy strict pass, but the trials use float money against DH-06, there are 8 type: ignore comments in scope, and 12 swallowing broad excepts rely on review because BLE, T20 and C90 aren't enabled.

credentials/ is cohesive with a narrow surface, but operations/ hosts the shared logger, application imports the worker, the worker imports api.main, and route_qualification serves as the trials' de facto library.
Most functions are short. The outliers are application/operations.py (501 lines), route_qualification.py (732) and browse_trial.run_trial (192 lines, 67 statements).
Most functions do one thing, with visible side effects. The exceptions are _settings_row's hidden insert, the monolithic trial runners and the list-cell state in maintenance_step.
operations/ mixes a long-running worker, operator CLIs, paid trials, the shared logger and a test fake. DH-03 names workers/, and the package docstring claims nothing in it runs at startup.

The lifecycle design is strong (heartbeat, bounded drain, worst-case ledger, AAD-bound encryption), but a drifted second readiness gate and a shared spend ledger whose path depends on the working directory undercut it.

Every module has a docstring, and comments explain invariants with requirement and decision IDs. Only 82 of 189 public definitions have docstrings, and a few comments are inaccurate or stand in for types.
Frozen dataclasses and Literals appear in places, but there are 35 Any-typed database and store handles, status strings needing 6 type: ignore comments, a cast and an anonymous binding object.

Errors are typed, with stable codes and fixed messages. But decryption errors leak past the store, boundary logs lose where the error happened, CLI exit codes disagree, and bootstrap has no recovery path.

Thorough fake-transport, tamper and readiness tests plus DB checks. The gaps: browse_trial.run_trial is never run offline, and the serve loop's drain, reconnect and final heartbeat are tested only against Docker Postgres.
Safe, well-explained code, but several rules are duplicated (pricing, readiness, ledger settlement, catalog status) and the copies have already drifted.

strengths.title: Secrets can't leak through serialization or repr
strengths.evidence: ResolvedCredential (services/agent/src/autobots/application/credentials/store.py:48-72) refuses pickling and hides its value in repr. Its docstring explains why: LangGraph's checkpoint serializer writes dataclasses and SecretStr in plaintext. EnvironmentCandidate hides its value too (precedence.py:15-21). Both are tested at services/agent/tests/test_credentials.py:142-166.

strengths.title: Authenticated encryption bound to row identity, and a master key that is never replaced
strengths.evidence: crypto.py:25-41 seals with a fresh nonce and associated data of workspace|provider|credential|version, and raises an error that carries no detail. master_key.py:15-43 creates the key with O_EXCL and 0600/0700 permissions, and refuses symlinks or open permissions. store.py:94-106 generates a key only when no encrypted row exists (SP-007). Tampering cases are tested at test_credentials.py:87-140.

strengths.title: Logs redact by default, and remote tracing is switched off at process start
strengths.evidence: operations/logs.py:12-25 redacts provider and tool keys, bearer tokens, JWTs and connection strings. Lines 54-67 keep only the exception type, and lines 93-105 clear LangSmith's cached settings. api/main.py:39-40, worker.py:316-317 and each trial's _main call these first. Tested at test_operations.py:64-79.

strengths.title: Paid calls are recorded at worst case before they are sent
strengths.evidence: route_qualification.py:115-176 keeps an fsync'd ledger guarded by flock and re-read under the lock. Lines 277-287 keep an unclear outcome charged at worst case, and lines 677-692 send nothing without --paid. Reports carry evidence_class and not_established (lines 648-669). browse_trial.py:51-54 and 256-257 record the start before the call, so the once-only trial can't repeat.

strengths.title: The worker lifecycle is deliberate and documented
strengths.evidence: worker.py:74-91 sends heartbeats on its own connection, so a long step can't make the worker look dead. Lines 102-122 drain within a bound, lines 158-169 write a final stopped heartbeat, and lines 264-281 keep a failing step from starving the next one. The module docstring (lines 1-11) explains why billed inference is opt-in.

strengths.title: Retention is scoped and ordered for crash safety
strengths.evidence: retention.py:101-123 pages by (updated_at, id), so refused runs can't crowd out later ones. Lines 64-89 remove bytes only after the rows commit, so a crash leaves bytes to retry, never a row pointing at nothing.

strengths.title: Tests pin duplicated tables to their source
strengths.evidence: test_schema_release.py:20-22 ties SHIPPED_MIGRATIONS and NEWEST_MIGRATION to supabase/migrations. test_route_qualification.py:339-343 requires a qualification route for every approved profile. precedence.py:1 shares its precedence fixtures with TypeScript (test_credentials.py:40).

strengths.title: Comments explain invariants, not syntax
strengths.evidence: application/operations.py:394-422 explains why sockets are only detached on macOS, and lines 102-107 explain why p95 rounds up. master_key.py:1 states the never-replace rule, and requirement and decision IDs trace the code to its sources throughout the area.

findings.title: Paid trials price calls with a second, float-based catalog parser

locations.note: Price in float USD; price_of reads prompt and completion only and drops every tiered override
the report records Price.__dict__ as catalog_price
the reasoning trial reuses price_of for the shared US$1 ledger
canonical Decimal parser: input_cache_write, internal_reasoning, per-request fee, tiers reachable under 32K

findings.impact: DH-06 forbids float arithmetic for money, and the two parsers of one catalog field already disagree. A route can bill reasoning tokens or cache writes above its completion rate, charge per request, or start a price tier below the qualification prompt size. Such a route is reserved below its real worst case in the ledgers that enforce the caps of Decisions 0009 and 0019. Any pricing change has to be made twice, and the application's tests exercise only one copy.
findings.recommendation: Price trial calls with the application's rules. `prepare` already calls validated_entry, so have it return the CatalogEntry, compute `worst_case_cost(entry.pricing, CONTEXT_TOKENS, OUTPUT_TOKENS)`, and refuse when it raises CostUnavailable. Record entry.pricing as the report's catalog_price, then delete Price and price_of, and move the override test (services/agent/tests/test_route_qualification.py:514-520) and the three price_of uses in services/agent/tests/test_reasoning_trial.py onto Pricing. Convert a reported cost with one Decimal ceiling helper; adapters/loop_middleware.py:276-278 does the same conversion with round(float).
findings.sketch:
operations/paid/pricing.py
  def worst_case(entry: CatalogEntry) -> int:      # integer micro-USD; refuses an unknown price
      return worst_case_cost(entry.pricing, CONTEXT_TOKENS, OUTPUT_TOKENS)
  def reported_micro_usd(message) -> int | None:   # Decimal(str(cost)) * 10**6, ROUND_CEILING
route_qualification.prepare(route, payload, max_tokens) -> tuple[PreparedAttempt, CatalogEntry]
preflight and reasoning_trial.run_trial: worst = worst_case(entry)
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06 (Python): exact decimal or integer monetary units, no float arithmetic for money. Decisions 0009 and 0019 S4 count calls at worst case. The shared parser is at least as conservative, so no cap is weakened.
findings.verifierNote: price_of, its three source call sites (route_qualification.py:616 and :656, reasoning_trial.py:211) and DH-06's ban on float money confirmed against catalog.parse_pricing. The recommendation now also covers the report's catalog_price field and the tests that use price_of; the override test sits at test_route_qualification.py:514-520.

findings.title: Routine admission re-implements the readiness gate and skips the schema check

locations.note: unattended_refusal checks adapter, storage and disk only, and parses the environment on every call
the comment says a routine waits on the same readiness a person would
person admission: database, schema, hold, adapter, storage and disk, through is_ready
the M14 check arranges only Storage down

findings.evidence:
```
async def unattended_refusal(connection: Any, store: Any) -> str | None:
    if not await adapter_qualified(connection):
        return "adapter_unqualified"
    storage = await storage_condition(store)
    ...
    minimum = int(os.environ.get("AUTOBOTS_MIN_FREE_BYTES", DEFAULT_MIN_FREE_BYTES))
    disk = disk_condition(Path(os.environ.get("AUTOBOTS_CONFIG_ROOT") or "."), minimum)
```
The API's _installation_conditions builds [database, schema, hold, adapter, storage, disk], and require_ready applies is_ready to it. It repeats the same two environment parses (operation_routes.py:87 and :95).
findings.impact: The worker's comment and DB check M14 promise one readiness. But when the code is newer than the database (schema_behind, Decision 0023 E2), a person's run is refused while the worker still evaluates and admits due routines. Every new blocking condition has to be added to two gates. Both gates re-read the environment on each call, so a malformed AUTOBOTS_MIN_FREE_BYTES fails every maintenance step and every admission. The worker logs only ValueError and skips retention.
findings.recommendation: Own installation readiness in one application function that takes a connection and the object store and returns the conditions, with its settings parsed once at process start. The API's require_ready and the worker's maintenance step both call it and refuse on the first blocking condition. Extend M14 to arrange schema_behind and a held install.
findings.sketch:
application/readiness.py
  @dataclass(frozen=True)
  class ReadinessSettings: data_root: Path; min_free_bytes: int     # from_environment(), once per process
  async def installation_conditions(connection, store, settings, probes=None) -> list[Condition]
  def first_blocking(conditions) -> Condition | None                 # BLOCKING minus NOT_BLOCKING
api.require_ready: refuse when first_blocking(await installation_conditions(...)) is not None
worker.maintenance_step: refused = first_blocking(...); log refused.code; skip routines, keep retention
findings.ruleCheck: This strengthens an admission guard (LM-07, Decision 0023 E2), and scheduling stays in Python, with nothing moved to Next.js.
findings.verifierNote: unattended_refusal checks the adapter, Storage and disk, and the hold is checked separately by is_held (worker.py:199), so schema is the one blocking condition a person's admission applies and a routine's doesn't. The M14 check (tests/db/major_check.py:337-359) arranges only Storage down, and Decision 0023 records an install that ran newer code on a database 14 migrations behind.

findings.title: Shared logging and process wiring live in the entry-point package

locations.note: says nothing here runs at service startup
API startup imports configure_logging and forbid_remote_tracing from operations.logs
one of 9 modules outside operations/ that import operations.logs
function-local import of operations.worker, used by the module-level CRONJOB at :181
goal_loop imports CRONJOB at module level, which closes the cycle
the worker imports api.main for provider_context_from_environment

findings.evidence:
```
async def _environment_check(connection: Any, workspace_id: UUID) -> str:
    """The worker's own readiness answer, so a scheduled and an asked-for occurrence agree."""
    from autobots.operations.worker import credential_check_from_environment

    return await credential_check_from_environment()(connection, workspace_id)
```
The package docstring says "Nothing here runs at service startup". Yet 9 modules outside operations/ import operations.logs (counted with grep): adapters (loop_middleware, result_stream), api (main, operation_routes) and application (operations, retention, goal_loop, routines, worker_inference). goal_loop imports cronjob_tool at module level, cronjob_tool imports the worker inside a function, and the worker imports goal_loop and api.main, which loads api.app and every router.
findings.impact: cronjob_tool → operations.worker → application.goal_loop → cronjob_tool is a cycle that only the function-local import keeps out of import time. To build its provider context, the worker process loads the FastAPI app factory and every router. Readers can't trust the package boundary that the docstring describes. The credential-check callable is also typed under the name CredentialCheck with two different signatures (routines.py:38, cronjob_tool.py:35).
findings.recommendation: Move logs.py to a leaf module that imports nothing from autobots. Move provider_context_from_environment and credential_check_from_environment to a composition module that api/main and the worker import. The object-store construction repeated in api/main.py:46-49 and worker.py:321-325 belongs there too. Pass the credential check into cronjob_tool from that composition root instead of the local import. Keep operations/, or DH-03's workers/, for entry points.
findings.sketch:
autobots/observability.py   redact, JsonFormatter, configure_logging, log_event, forbid_remote_tracing (no autobots imports)
autobots/configuration.py   provider_context_from_environment(), object_store_from_environment(), credential_check(context)
operations/worker.py        imports configuration, never api.main
application/cronjob_tool.py receives its credential check from the registry's composition; no local import
findings.ruleCheck: DH-03 lists src/autobots/{api,domain,application,adapters,workers,graphs,contracts}, and DH-06 asks for explicit ownership and narrow interfaces. The move changes no behavior.
findings.verifierNote: The nine importers of operations.logs, the function-local import and worker.py:29 confirmed. The cycle is now named exactly: goal_loop.py:47 imports cronjob_tool, whose lazy import of the worker would bring goal_loop back at import time.

findings.title: application/operations.py mixes six concerns in 501 lines

locations.note: constants for readiness, backups, the catalog and occurrences are interleaved
backup manifests and restore logs, read synchronously
NOT_BLOCKING and is_ready, far from BLOCKING at :75
the async status route calls the blocking backup readers

findings.evidence:
One module holds six concerns:
- the admission gate: Condition, BLOCKING, the database, storage, disk, queue and worker conditions, and is_ready
- operator values: ProbeTimes, counts, migrations, disk bytes, the checkpoint adapter and catalog timing
- backup-file parsing: backup_age_hours and restore_history
- routine occurrences
- host socket introspection: loopback_only
- the jobs-chart query: _JOB_HOURS

api/operation_routes.py imports 22 names from it (lines 14-37). backup_age_hours and restore_history glob and read files with blocking calls, and they run inside the async local-status route.
findings.impact: The admission gate is reviewed and changed amid chart SQL and file parsing, and its two halves, BLOCKING at line 75 and NOT_BLOCKING with is_ready at lines 492-501, sit 400 lines apart. Each local-status request also does blocking file reads on the event loop, which DH-06 says to keep off it; the files are small, so this costs little today.
findings.recommendation: Split the module by concern, keeping names importable through re-exports during the move. Call the backup readers through asyncio.to_thread.
findings.sketch:
application/readiness.py         Condition (Literal name and state), BLOCKING, NOT_BLOCKING, is_ready, RequiredSchema,
                                 database/storage/disk/queue/worker conditions, installation_conditions
application/operation_values.py  ProbeTimes, QueueCounts, queue_counts, live_workers, applied_migrations,
                                 stored_bytes, disk_bytes, checkpoint_adapter, timed_catalog, loopback_only
application/backups.py           backup_age_hours, restore_history -> list[RestoreRow], called through to_thread
application/activity.py          job_hours with _JOB_HOURS, delayed_occurrences -> list[DelayedRow]
findings.ruleCheck: DH-06: small cohesive modules, and keep blocking work off the async event loop.
findings.verifierNote: Six concerns and their line ranges confirmed. operation_routes.py imports 22 names from the module, not 20. The speculation that the mix explains the worker's second gate was dropped; the backup readers do run synchronously in the async route.

findings.title: Paid-call reservation and settlement are hand-rolled five times and have drifted

locations.note: cancellation: reserves, then settles in finally
entries are dict[str, Any], and state is any string
planned_calls hard-codes 13 calls, apart from the fixture list at 496-509

findings.evidence:
```
# route_qualification.py:281-286
        except BaseException:
            self.ledger.settle(entry, None, "uncertain")
            raise
        self.ledger.settle(entry, cost, "settled" if cost is not None else "usage_unreported")
# reasoning_trial.py:187-191
    except Exception:
        ledger.settle(entry, None, "uncertain")
```
reasoning_trial then settles the same unreported outcome as "no_reported_charge".
findings.impact: The copies already disagree. An interrupted or cancelled reasoning-trial call is left as "reserved" instead of "uncertain"; committed() still holds it at worst case, so the cap is safe, but the record no longer says what happened. One outcome has two names in a ledger file that is shared with the install's goals, which add "not_started" and "run_not_finished" (scripts/persistent_install.py:331-683). Adding a fixture without also editing planned_calls makes the preflight undercount.
findings.recommendation: Give Ledger one async context manager. It reserves, settles as "uncertain" on any BaseException and re-raises, and otherwise settles from the reported charge. Type the entries as a dataclass with a Literal state. Derive the planned calls from a fixture table that also drives Corpus.run.
findings.sketch:
LedgerState = Literal['reserved', 'settled', 'usage_unreported', 'uncertain', 'not_started', 'run_not_finished']
@dataclass class LedgerEntry: label: str; worst_case: int; reported: int | None; state: LedgerState; at: str
@asynccontextmanager
async def charge(self, label: str, worst: int) -> AsyncIterator[Receipt]:
    entry = self.reserve(label, worst)
    try: receipt = Receipt(); yield receipt
    except BaseException: self.settle(entry, None, 'uncertain'); raise
    self.settle(entry, receipt.reported, 'settled' if receipt.reported is not None else 'usage_unreported')
FIXTURE_CALLS = {'plain_text': 1, ..., 'continuation': 2}   # planned_calls sums it
findings.ruleCheck: Two rules are kept: Decision 0009 holds a call at its worst case until it settles, and DH-06 propagates cancellation after cleanup. Unifying on BaseException brings the reasoning trial in line.
findings.verifierNote: Five reserve-and-settle copies confirmed (route_qualification.py:277, 289, 392 and 471; reasoning_trial.py:180). Only the reasoning trial catches Exception, and persistent_install.py settles with not_started and run_not_finished. The impact now notes that committed() keeps a reserved entry at worst case.

findings.title: The credential store lets decryption errors escape, so seven callers compensate

locations.note: translates MasterKeyUnavailable but not unseal's CredentialDecryptionError

findings.evidence:
```
        try:
            key = load_master_key(self._key_path)
        except MasterKeyUnavailable as error:
            raise CredentialStorageUnavailable("the master key is unavailable") from error
        aad = associated_data(workspace_id, self._provider, row[0], row[1])
        plaintext = unseal(key, Sealed(bytes(row[2]), bytes(row[3]), bytes(row[4])), aad)
```
Six handlers catch (CredentialStorageUnavailable, CredentialDecryptionError) together, and revalidate re-raises one as the other.
findings.impact: Every caller has to know about an exception from the lower crypto module and treat it like the store's own. A new caller that catches only CredentialStorageUnavailable would turn a damaged row into an internal error, because settings_routes.as_api_error maps only the store's types. The boundary also leaks the other way: provider_settings.py:205-209 and tool_key_settings.py:125 mark credential rows deleted by writing the store's table directly.
findings.recommendation: Translate CredentialDecryptionError inside load_active, as it already does for MasterKeyUnavailable. Raise a store-level subclass such as CredentialUnreadable(CredentialStorageUnavailable), so the existing handlers and settings_routes.as_api_error catch it while worker_inference's type-only log still tells a damaged row from a missing key. Then drop CredentialDecryptionError from the seven handlers. Add ProviderCredentialStore.delete_active to replace the two direct writes, and rename resolve_for_attempt_blocked_check (store.py:75), which is a guard, to require_usable.
findings.ruleCheck: SP-007: a missing or wrong master key with encrypted rows stays an error, never a replacement. Error codes and fixed messages are unchanged.
findings.verifierNote: All seven handler sites and both direct status writes confirmed, and every caller treats the two errors alike. The recommendation now raises a subclass, because worker_inference.py:77 logs only the exception type and a plain translation would hide a damaged row behind 'storage unavailable'.

findings.title: Boundary handlers log only the exception class, and retention's failure log omits the workspace

locations.note: the same handler, copied in both()
the formatter keeps only the exception type

findings.evidence:
```
        except Exception as error:
            log_event(logger, "retention.failed", logging.WARNING, error=type(error).__name__)
```
JsonFormatter writes `record.exc_info[0].__name__` and nothing else, and every handler passes `error=type(error).__name__`. So a failing worker step logs `{"event": "worker.step_failed", "error": "KeyError"}`, with no step, module or line. The success line for retention carries `workspace=`, but the failure line doesn't.
findings.impact: A recurring failure in the long-running worker or in readiness can only be located by reproducing it, and a retention failure can't be tied to a workspace. DH-06 asks to preserve causes in private logs. Dropping the message is right, since it can carry a connection string, but that doesn't require dropping the location too.
findings.recommendation: Add error_fields(error) to the logging module. It returns the exception class plus the innermost autobots frame as module:function:line, with no message text. Use it at these seven sites; the handler copied into both() can share one helper with serve. Add workspace=workspace_id to retention.failed.
findings.ruleCheck: LM-07 and test_operations.py:64-79 keep messages out of logs. A frame location carries no message, secret or identifier, so both still hold.
findings.verifierNote: The seven broad handlers that log only the class (worker.py:89, 143 and 276; operations.py:153, 205 and 356; retention.py:171) and the formatter's type-only rule confirmed. The worker step and retention handlers gain the most, since the readiness events already name what they probed.

findings.title: Status vocabularies are bare strings, held together by six type: ignore comments

```

class Condition:
    name: str

...
```

findings.impact: mypy strict can't catch a misspelled state or code inside the application. run_intent's codes are compared with != "ready" and looked up in INTENT_FAILURES, which raises KeyError for any code it lacks. The credential check that returns these codes is typed Awaitable[str], under one alias name with two signatures (routines.py:38, cronjob_tool.py:35). findings.recommendation: Type each vocabulary once, with Literal aliases or StrEnums for condition name and state, auth status, catalog status, credential source and run intent. Where provider_settings already imports contracts.settings, reuse its AuthStatus, CatalogStatus and CredentialSource. Narrow the database strings once, when the settings row is read. Then remove the ignores.

findings.title: Three catalog-availability checks disagree, and one has no caller

locations.note: timed_catalog: 3 s; catches TimeoutError, OSError and ValueError
openrouter_availability: the same logic, with no caller (git grep)
catalog_status: no timeout; catches OSError only
reply.json() raises ValueError on a non-JSON 200

findings.impact: When the catalog answers 200 with a body that isn't JSON, Operations shows "unavailable", but GET /v1/settings/model-providers and GET /v1/models end in an internal error. Settings also waits up to the HTTP client's 15 s, where Operations waits 3 s. The dead copy is a third one to maintain.
findings.recommendation: Write one application helper that fetches within a time limit, maps every expected failure to unavailable, and returns the status, payload and elapsed time. Use it in Operations and in ProviderSettings.status and models. Delete openrouter_availability.
findings.ruleCheck: MP-04 and SP-007: catalog status stays independent of authentication, and no model call is added.
findings.verifierNote: catalog_fetcher catches only httpx.HTTPError and calls reply.json() unguarded, so a non-JSON 200 raises ValueError: Operations maps it to unavailable, while ProviderSettings.status and models let it escape. git grep finds no caller of openrouter_availability.

findings.title: Owner bootstrap can stop between its two writes, and reports only the exception class

locations.note: an Auth user, then a workspace, under one generic handler
Auth admin API create; not idempotent

findings.title: browse_trial.run_trial does the whole trial inline, and its report assembly has no offline test

locations.note: 'started' is written before the paid call, which blocks a rerun
the report is built by zipping rows with column tuples
imports refuse_repeat, TrialModel, hosts and inside, never run_trial

findings.evidence: browse_trial.run_trial does the whole trial in one body. It creates an Expert, builds a binding, admits a run, checks the frozen Sol route, claims the job twice, drives the gateway, approves, writes the start record, reads invocations and tool uses, and assembles the report. The module says "It runs in no verification profile" (browse_trial.py:13), as US-14.16#1 requires, and no test calls run_trial. US-14.16 is DONE, so the trial has run once. reasoning_trial.run_trial, which test_reasoning_trial.py exercises with a fake transport, mutates one TrialResult across eight early returns.
findings.impact: The code that spends the once-only Sol trial budget (Decision 0019 S6) runs only live. It matters when the owner asks for a repeat: a defect in report assembly after the call, such as a zip(strict=True) column mismatch, would surface after money is spent and after the start record is written, and that record refuses another repeat without the owner. The environment mutation also leaks into whatever runs next in the process.
findings.recommendation: Before any owner-requested repeat, split the browse trial into named steps and make the report a pure function over typed rows, unit-tested with fixed rows; that needs no database, executor or model. Keep run_trial itself out of the verification profiles, as US-14.16#1 states. In reasoning_trial, return early through one small stop type instead of mutating the result in eight places.
findings.sketch:
async def run_trial(...):                                        # about 30 lines
    run, policy = await _admit_trial_run(db, workspace, actor)    # Expert, admission, Sol check
    pending = await _execute(db, await _claim(db, run), runtime)  # gateway inside middleware.active()
    await _approve(db, workspace, actor, run)
    _write(out, started(run)); result = await _execute(db, await _claim(db, run), runtime)
    return build_report(run, route, result, await _read_spend(db, run), executor.log)
def build_report(run, route, result, rows: SpendRows, log) -> dict    # pure; unit-tested with fixed rows
reasoning_trial: _first_call(...) -> Reply | Stop; _continue(...) -> Reply | Stop; _compare(...) -> TrialResult
findings.ruleCheck: Decision 0019 S6 (one live trial), US-14.16#1 (no verification profile) and the --owner-requested-repeat refusal stay. DH-06 and model-gateway.md make fake transports and pure units the default test path.
findings.verifierNote: 192 lines, 67 statements, 7 parameters, 12 inline imports and the os.environ write confirmed; no test calls browse_trial.run_trial. Lowered to low because US-14.16 is DONE and a repeat needs the owner. The recommendation now unit-tests a pure report instead of running the trial in the db profile, which US-14.16#1 keeps out of verification.

findings.title: _settings_row inserts on every read, and two writers call it only for that insert

locations.note: run_intent, the gate before each model call and each routine admission

findings.evidence:
```
    async def _settings_row(self, workspace_id: UUID, lock: bool = False) -> tuple[int, str, Any]:
        await self._connection.execute(
            "insert into app_private.provider_settings (workspace_id) values (%s) "
            "on conflict (workspace_id) do nothing",
            (workspace_id,),
        )
```
revalidate and mark_invalid call `await self._settings_row(workspace_id)` and ignore what it returns, so that the following _record update finds a row.
findings.impact: This getter also writes. Every status read and every run-intent check, which runs before each model call and each routine admission, issues an insert. The runtime role already holds insert on the table, so the cost is clarity rather than privilege, but the two calls that discard the result hide why they exist. The positional boolean `lock` is what ruff's FBT001 flags.
findings.recommendation: Split the function. _ensure_settings_row serves the writers (save_credential, disconnect, revalidate, mark_invalid). _read_settings(workspace_id, *, for_update=False) returns the table defaults (version 0, "missing", no validated_at) when no row exists.
findings.ruleCheck: SP-014 and MP-05: version-checked settings mutations keep their row lock, and reads stop writing.
findings.verifierNote: The insert-then-select and its callers confirmed. Lowered to low: the runtime role is granted insert on provider_settings anyway, and an insert that conflicts writes no row. The table defaults the recommendation relies on are version 0, 'missing' and a null validated_at (supabase/migrations/20261105000005_provider_settings.sql:2-8).

findings.title: Entry points disagree on configuration checks, refusals and exit codes

locations.note: a malformed --only raises an uncaught ValueError

findings.evidence:
A missing AUTOBOTS_DATABASE_URL gets a different outcome in each entry point:
- bootstrap_owner: exit 2 with "ERROR: set ..."
- concept_seed: exit 2 with "REFUSED: ..."
- worker: exit 1 through SystemExit
- browse_trial: a KeyError traceback

Refusal prefixes vary too: "ERROR: bootstrap was refused", "REFUSED, nothing sent", "REFUSED, nothing further sent" and "REFUSED:". The trials and the worker also write JSON log lines to the same stderr.
findings.impact: Wrappers and runbooks can't tell "not configured" from "refused" the same way across entry points, and bad arguments surface as tracebacks. bootstrap_owner documents exit 2 for missing configuration, matching what AGENTS.md uses for verify.py's unavailable prerequisite, but the other entry points don't follow it. No script tells these codes apart today, so the cost is operator confusion.
findings.recommendation: Add a small shared CLI helper with three parts: require_env(*names), which exits 2; refuse(reason), with one stderr format and exit 1; and argparse type= parsers for UUIDs and name=count pairs. Library code raises typed errors, such as seed's missing owner, instead of SystemExit. Keep stdout JSON as the result contract that the wrappers parse.
findings.ruleCheck: Follows the AGENTS.md exit codes (0 passed, 1 failed, 2 prerequisite unavailable) and bootstrap_owner's own docstring. scripts/qualify_identity.py:60 reads stdout JSON, which stays unchanged.
findings.verifierNote: Each exit path confirmed, including the uncaught ValueError from a malformed --only. Lowered to low: the qualifiers only test for a nonzero exit and read the JSON on stdout, so nothing depends on 1 versus 2 yet.

findings.title: Query rows and database or store handles cross module boundaries untyped

locations.note: column names written in the SQL and again for zip
an ObjectStore Protocol already exists (without ping)

findings.evidence: The scope has 35 untyped handle parameters (26 `connection: Any`, 1 `pool: Any`, 8 `store: Any`) and 36 lines in six files that index query rows by position. Both were counted with a regex over the 18 files, the second matching row, record, found, active, zone, present and result indexed by a digit, and fetchone())[0]. `delayed_occurrences(...) -> list[tuple[Any, ...]]` is consumed as row[0] to row[3] by api/operation_routes.py. Yet persistence/rows.py says "A row is never a public response; adapters convert it explicitly", and adapters/checkpoints.py:70 already uses psycopg's dict_row.
findings.impact: Reordering a select silently changes meaning in another module. mypy can't check the store's ping and remove or a connection's methods, so the ObjectStore Protocol and the row convention protect nothing here.
findings.recommendation: Where rows leave a module, return a small dataclass or TypedDict, using psycopg's class_row or dict_row. Type store parameters as ObjectStore extended with ping, or as a narrow Pingable protocol. Type connections as psycopg.AsyncConnection or a narrow protocol.
findings.ruleCheck: Follows persistence/rows.py's convention and DH-06's ban on broad untyped dictionaries. Rows stay separate from DTOs.
findings.verifierNote: Handle count confirmed at 35. The positional-index count is 36 lines with the wider name set (29 with row, record and fetchone() alone), not 35, so occurrences is 71.

findings.title: The readiness lists carry a truncated comment and an over-attributed decision range, and a DB check patches them

locations.note: 'Add the one a required new migration creates.'
cites migrations 38 to 53 to Decision 0023 E2
the count is null with neither history table present
E2: the lists cover migrations 38 to 49, for a database with no readable history

findings.evidence:
```
# The relations a release can't run without. Add the one a required new migration creates.
    # Migrations 38 to 53 (Decision 0023 E2), for a database with no readable history.
# A migration can add only columns, which a relation check can't see. The newest code relies on.
```
Decision 0023 E2 names migrations 38 to 49. applied_migration_count() returns null when neither history table exists, and schema_condition then lets the lists decide (operations.py:177-185), so they are what shows such a database as behind.
findings.impact: The comment credits E2 with a range it doesn't state, and the truncated sentence leaves the column list's purpose unclear. Nothing in the code says that the lists exist for a database whose history can't be counted, which is why each later migration still adds an entry. Because database_conditions reads the module globals, the DB check reassigns operations.REQUIRED_COLUMNS to exercise them.
findings.recommendation: Replace the three comments with one docstring that says what the lists are for (a database whose applied history can't be counted, Decision 0023 E2, extended to each later migration) and finishes the column list's sentence. Pass a RequiredSchema argument that defaults to the constants, so tests don't have to patch module state.
findings.ruleCheck: Aligns the comment with Decision 0023 E2 and keeps the practice of citing decisions in comments.
findings.verifierNote: The truncated sentence, the 38-to-53 citation and the patch in tests/db/review_check.py:177-180 confirmed. The original claim that the applied count makes per-migration entries unnecessary was withdrawn: the count is null without a history table, and then only the lists can show the database behind.

findings.evidence: serve, _beat and the final heartbeat each run `async with await psycopg.AsyncConnection.connect(config.database_url, autocommit=True) as connection:`. tests/db/operations_worker.py drives serve against a disposable database. both() already has three unit tests (services/agent/tests/test_worker_inference.py:1031-1081), and _run_step takes its connection as an argument, yet no unit test exercises the drain. maintenance_step keeps its state in `last_retention: list[float] = []` and `said: list[str] = []`.

findings.verifierNote: The three self-opened connections and the missing drain test confirmed. both() is not untested: test_worker_inference.py has three tests for it, so that location was replaced, and the drain test needs no refactor.
